facts.label: Virtualization
facts.question: How will you run the VMs?

pages: Hi {name}! I'm Mauro, one of the maintainers of Kairos, and this is KAI, our armadillo mascot. In this workshop you build and run an immutable Kubernetes cluster, one stage at a time. You type every command yourself, because that is how it sticks. KAI helps when you get stuck.
An immutable system treats the operating system like an application image. You never patch it in place. You build a new image, boot into it, and go back to the previous one if it misbehaves.
Why? Upgrades are predictable, rollbacks are instant, and every machine is identical, so nothing drifts.

Kairos is a fully open source CNCF Sandbox project. It turns the Linux distribution of your choice into an immutable, image-based system with Kubernetes built in. Bare metal, VMs, edge and public cloud, we have you covered!
This workshop is brought to you by our generous patron, [Spectro Cloud](https://www.spectrocloud.com/solutions/kairos-support).

options.label: Windows
options.text: This is not game over. Zen is not available on Windows, so you play Master.

questions.title: How will you run the VMs?

options.label: Zen
options.text: kairos-lab creates and boots the VMs and sets up their network for you, so you can focus on Kairos.

options.label: Master
options.text: You bring your own virtualization software. You must know how to create a VM, give it a network that is shared with your computer (or use tunneling), and make sure the VM can reach the internet. Stuck? Ask KAI for a TIP: a ready prompt you paste into your favorite AI assistant.

help.label: Not sure?
help.text: x86_64 means amd64. arm64 or aarch64 means arm64.

questions.title: Which container runtime?
questions.text: It is your choice, but Docker is the more battle-tested one for this workshop.

notes.text: If you already have a runtime, `kairos-lab setup` uses it. If you have none, it asks before it installs one. Docker is the default. Run `kairos-lab setup -runtime podman` to use Podman.

steps.title: Install kairos-lab
steps.line: Let's get kairos-lab onto your machine.

blocks.md:
`kairos-lab` only works on Linux and macOS. On Windows, use your own
virtualization software instead.

blocks.code:
brew tap kairos-io/kairos
brew install kairos-lab

git clone https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos-lab.git && cd kairos-lab
go build -o kairos-lab ./cmd/kairos-lab

blocks.md: Or download the binaries from the [releases page](https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos-lab/releases).
On macOS, the downloaded binary is not signed. Authorize it in System Settings > Privacy & Security after the first run.

check.prompt: The kairos-lab command is available in a new terminal.

steps.title: Run kairos-lab setup
steps.line: One command gets your tools ready.

help.goal: Run the first-time setup of kairos-lab and AuroraBoot

blocks.md:
If `kairos-lab setup` installed the container runtime for you, it does not
start it. On macOS, open Docker Desktop once (or run `podman machine init` and
`podman machine start`), then run `kairos-lab setup` again to finish.

Detects your package manager and installs `qemu` if it is missing.

It also gets you `auroraboot`, the command you use in [stage 3](stage:build-image) to
turn an image you build into an ISO. For that it needs a container runtime,
Docker or Podman. It pulls the AuroraBoot container image and installs a small
`auroraboot` command in `~/.local/bin`.

steps.title: Check the auroraboot command
steps.line: Let's make sure the new tool answers.

help.goal: Check that the auroraboot command works

blocks.md: Check that the command works:

check.prompt: The auroraboot command is available in a new terminal.

fail.md:
If your shell says the command is not found, `~/.local/bin` is not on your
`PATH`. `kairos-lab setup` tells you what to add.

steps.title: Pull the image
steps.line: Bring AuroraBoot over as a container image.

blocks.md:
If you are using your own virtualization software, `kairos-lab setup` does not
run for you, so you need to get AuroraBoot yourself. There are two ways:

- Run the AuroraBoot container image. It needs a container runtime, Docker or
  Podman. This works on Linux and on macOS.
- On Linux only, build AuroraBoot locally and run it as a normal command.

Wherever the workshop says `auroraboot build-iso ...`, you either run the
container or use your local build instead. The examples below are the command
from the end of [stage 3](stage:build-image).

check.prompt: The quay.io/kairos/auroraboot:latest image is present in your container runtime.

steps.title: Run the container
steps.line: A trial run for later. You can skip it for now.

blocks.md: You do not need to run this now. You will use it at the end of stage 3.
This is the same as `auroraboot build-iso --output ./build stage-2:v1.0.0`:

blocks.code:
mkdir -p build && docker run -it --rm \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  -v $PWD/build:/result \
  quay.io/kairos/auroraboot:latest \
  build-iso --output /result stage-2:v1.0.0

blocks.md:
The Docker socket lets AuroraBoot find the image you built locally, and
`$PWD/build` is where the ISO ends up.

Podman has trouble using a locally built image, so stage 3 has you push your
image to a temporary public registry first (see
[Using Podman on MacOS](stage:build-image#alternative-using-podman-on-macos)). Once
you have done that, run AuroraBoot like this:

blocks.code:
mkdir -p build && sudo podman run -it --rm \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:Z \
  -v $PWD/build:/result \
  quay.io/kairos/auroraboot:latest \
  build-iso --output /result ttl.sh/stage-2:24h

steps.title: Build it locally (Linux only)
steps.line: Prefer a plain command? You can build it yourself.

blocks.md:
Use this if you would rather have a plain `auroraboot` command than run the
container.

**Do not build AuroraBoot on macOS. Use the container instead.** AuroraBoot is
built for Linux. To make an ISO it calls Linux tools (`xorriso`, `mtools`,
`mkfs.fat`, `mksquashfs`), it creates files owned by root, and it expects
boot files that only exist inside its container image. macOS has none of
that, so a build made there will not give you a working `auroraboot`. The
container is a Linux system with everything in place, which is why Docker and
Podman work on macOS.

steps.title: Build AuroraBoot
steps.line: Build AuroraBoot on your Linux machine.

blocks.md:
You need:

- Go, at the version in AuroraBoot's [`go.mod`](https://github.com/kairos-io/AuroraBoot/blob/main/go.mod)
  (1.26 at the time of writing).
- Node.js with npm, to build the web UI that is embedded in the binary.
- A C compiler, because one dependency (SQLite) is built with cgo.
- The tools AuroraBoot calls while it builds an ISO: at least `xorriso`,
  `mtools`, `dosfstools` and `squashfs-tools`. The container image installs a
  longer list (see the [`Dockerfile`](https://github.com/kairos-io/AuroraBoot/blob/main/Dockerfile)),
  because it also builds raw disks and UKIs. If a build complains about a
  missing tool, install it.

Build it:

blocks.code:
git clone https://github.com/kairos-io/AuroraBoot.git
cd AuroraBoot
make build

blocks.md: `make build` builds the web UI and then the Go binary, `./auroraboot`.

steps.title: Run your local build
steps.line: Try your local build. Save this one for later.

blocks.md:
You do not need to run this now. You will use it at the end of stage 3.

Run it as root, because it changes file ownership to root while it unpacks the
image. This is the same as the container command above:
The files in `./build` belong to root.

fail.md:
If the build stops with `could not find any shim file to copy`, the image does
not include a shim. The container carries a fallback for that case and a local
build does not, so use the container for that image.
